extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; aspiring writers and conversationalists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice (in essay form) about what makes agreeable conversation and the typical character/vices of news-writing, plus guidance on using analogy effectively in exposition. Useful to writers aiming for readable prose or convincing instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conversation (punch metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation is like a punch composed of spirit (wit), acid juices (pungency/raillery), sugar (luscious adulation and complaisance), and water (easy, artless talk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ingredients in balance: too much wit (spirit) overpowers and astonishes but does not please; unmixed acidity (satire) distorts and repels; sugar (meekness/courtesy) alone soon palls and must temper harsher qualities; water (plain, easy talk) can be used alone to inform and please the ignorant. The long-pleasing companion tempers satire with civility and allays wit's heat with humble chat, producing 'inoffensive copiousness' rather than showy brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogy and parallels in instruction/writing
rubrics_metrics.description: To teach or illustrate, explain the unknown by resemblance to something already known; parallels are the most popular and efficacious art of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer literal/real parallels (e.g., poetry and painting) when you need conviction and truth, because they rest on genuine likeness; fanciful or fortuitous parallels may please and exhibit ingenuity but are less convincing and carry less truth. Always connect new material to familiar images to facilitate comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-writing: incentives, methods, and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many modern news-writers aim not to be studied but merely to be read; the profession often prizes shamelessness and indifference to truth over genius, knowledge, industry, or sprightliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware (satirically) that popular news-writing tends toward sensationalism and fabrication: inventing or exaggerating expected battles, recounting tales of cruelty to awaken attention, and sometimes manufacturing letters or reports. In wartime this tendency is amplified because readers want flattering national narratives. The essay warns this practice diminishes the public love of truth and encourages credulity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain diction for informing ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the aim is to inform those ignorant of a subject, the plainest diction is most pleasing and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve wit and ornate language for moments of idleness or pride; for practical instruction or conveying necessary knowledge, favor simple, artless language (the 'water' of punch). Fancy and embellishment create artificial wants and are unnecessary when clarity and instruction are the goals.
